goals: One correct answer per question, split by property and season, in their voice, owned by them, kept whether or not they spend another dollar.
Settle the aurora date difference between the Wedgewood special (c14) and the Bear Lodge rooms page (c19).
Make the season flip happen on the date rather than by someone remembering, driven by a dated calendar file (c7, c14, c16, c19).
Put the twenty highest-traffic answers on one printed page per property per season, taped to each desk, reprinted the day the season turns.
Give every answer a named owner, a source and a review date, and make an unreviewed answer LOOK unreviewed instead of quietly aging.
Start an ask log on day one so the next decision is made on their numbers, measured through the August 21 flip (c14) and the mid-September Golden Bear close (c16).

components.name: Answer cards, one text file per answer, in a private repository they own
components.why: Version history, who changed what and when, and a one-click revert come free with the repository. The change log requirement met by the storage choice instead of a feature we would have to write and they would have to trust.

components.name: Card Check
components.why: A few hundred lines that runs on every save and refuses to publish a broken card set. Required fields, date windows that parse, no card holding both an answer and a live lookup, no two cards claiming the same question for the same property and season, quoted policy text still matching the published page, no review date already past. These rules ARE the product.

components.name: Season Calendar, one dated file
components.why: Four windows and a date comparison. Writing the two aurora windows side by side is what forces the c14 versus c19 difference into the open on day one.

components.name: Book Builder and the Desk Book site
components.why: Eleventy does the boring part. What we build is the per-property and per-season page shape, the expiry banding, and the change history. A wiki would hold the words and would not hold the season, the property split or the expiry.

components.name: Shift Sheet renderer
components.why: The PDF engine is bought. What we build is the judgment, which twenty cards, in what order, and the rule that an out-of-date card is never printed. A first-class output with its own build target.

components.name: Card editing form in the browser (Decap CMS)
components.why: Nobody at a hotel should learn a developer tool to fix a check-out time.

components.name: Hosting and reader access (Cloudflare Pages plus Access)
components.why: A pre-built site is pennies to host with nothing to keep alive. Access control at the edge is a setting. Internal operating policy needs a door, not an identity system.

components.name: Ask Log (Workers plus D1)
components.why: The host and store are bought. We build the FIELD LIST, because those fields are what later decides whether Desk Search is worth funding. Get them wrong now and the evidence does not exist in six weeks. No guest names, no room numbers, no personal data.

components.name: The find box
components.why: Plain word matching in the browser across each card's question and its other phrasings. No service, no request, no waiting. Also the one place a smarter match would ever slot in later.

components.name: Seed content, their published FAQ and property pages
components.why: Already written, already permissioned, already in their voice, and unusually good.

components.name: The desk printer and the tape
components.why: The sheet is the highest-adoption artifact and needs no procurement. If the only thing that ever gets used is the paper, this still paid for itself in a way the desk can feel.

design.property_scoping: Property is a setting, never an inference. Each desk machine is bookmarked to its own address. A card whose properties list excludes that property is not on the page at all. Where two properties answer differently, that is TWO CARDS, never one card with a paragraph of exceptions, because exceptions are what a tired clerk skips.
design.season_flip: The Season Calendar holds every window with real start and end dates. At build time the site writes every card's window into the page. In the browser the card is shown or hidden by one comparison of today's date against that window. No toggle for anyone to forget and no model involved. An editor can preview any date with one click, which is how the August 21 flip gets rehearsed before it happens. Card Check refuses to publish when two windows describing the same season disagree.
design.staleness: Every card carries last_reviewed and review_by. The build stamps a status computed from today: live, expiring within thirty days, or past review. A past-review card STAYS VISIBLE, because hiding the only answer a clerk has helps nobody, and it renders inside a band that says plainly it is past review with the owner's name on it. It is dropped from the printed sheet automatically, so a stale answer never gets taped to a desk. A card degrades loudly or it does not degrade.
design.policy_not_state_boundary: Structural, not a warning nobody reads. ONE, there is no field a live number could go in. A card that would need one can't be written and Card Check rejects the attempt. TWO, there is a check_live field instead, which names where to look rather than answering, and a card holding both an answer and a check_live is blocked at publish. THREE, every page and the printed sheet carry one standing line saying the book holds policy and how-to, never anything that changes today. FOUR, and this is the one that actually holds, THERE IS NO PIPE. Nothing connects to a booking or property system, so there is no channel through which a stale live number could ever arrive.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: That the operational long tail, the questions a desk actually gets that are nowhere on the website, can be written down inside the weeks this budget buys. Parking, pets, luggage hold, accessible rooms, maintenance at 2am, what to do when the van is full.
riskiest_assumption.why_riskiest: If that knowledge is only in one veteran's head, the editorial work is not part of the project, it IS the project, at a size nobody has scoped. What ships instead is a nicely built reprint of the FAQ the desk already has. Every other risk resizes the prize. This one invalidates the design.
riskiest_assumption.spike: Two days on site, BEFORE anything is signed. Day one, sit at the Wedgewood desk across a shift change and tally every question, marking each as already answered by the published FAQ, answered by a veteran from memory, or answered from something already written. Day two, ask the two longest-serving supervisors to write out their top twenty questions unaided and separately, then check how many of those forty answers exist in writing anywhere. The pass mark is agreed in writing before day one starts.
riskiest_assumption.timebox: Two days on site plus half a day to write it up. Fixed.

design.estimates_total_days: 20 to 35 working days end to end, medium confidence. The spike collapses roughly half the band.
design.walking_skeleton: Week one, three real answers travelling the whole path once. Check-in and check-out (c8), the summer late check-out rule (c7), the 24-hour cancellation notice (c13). A named editor edits one in the browser form and saves. Card Check runs and the site rebuilds. The Wedgewood page shows summer cards in season, and the aurora cards as not yet in season with the date they arrive. One sheet comes out of the desk printer. A clerk types 'late checkout' into the find box and the card appears with no wait. One row lands in the Ask Log and shows up in the owner's weekly email on Monday. Every piece is real. The only thing that is small is the number of cards.
design.seam_for_conditional_next: The find box is the seam and it is the only thing that would move. Desk Search would replace what happens inside that one box, matching by meaning rather than exact wording, with property and season still applied first, and still returning their own card word for word. Nothing else changes. The log's stored questions become the test it has to pass.

architecture.caption: Their answers, dated and owned, become one page per property and one sheet of paper per shift. Anything that changes today stays where it already lives, because nothing here connects to it. What the desk looks for and does not find comes back to the owner every Monday.

prd.headline: A first-week front desk hire at Wedgewood, Sophie Station or Bear Lodge gives the answer a ten-year veteran would give, in either season

success_metrics.metric: Days from a seasonal front-of-house hire's start date to their first shift working the desk without a supervisor on the floor
success_metrics.baseline: NONE EXISTS. Built in the first two weeks from their own schedules.
success_metrics.target: 20 percent reduction against the measured baseline, or we report plainly that it did not move. If the roster is mostly returning staff this metric is DROPPED at kickoff and the fee is cut, rather than quietly restated as something easier to hit.
success_metrics.timeframe: Baseline weeks 1 and 2. Honest caveat, few new front-of-house people start in September, so the fair read is the spring hire-up. Phase 1 establishes the baseline, it does not claim the result.

success_metrics.metric: Interruptions to a supervisor or veteran per shift, on questions the published answer set already covers
success_metrics.baseline: NONE EXISTS. Measured before anything is built, using a paper tally at each of the three desks for two weeks.
success_metrics.target: 30 percent fewer covered-question interruptions in weeks 7 and 8 than in the weeks 1 and 2 baseline, on the same three desks.
success_metrics.timeframe: Baseline weeks 1-2, comparison weeks 7-8, spanning the August 21 flip.

success_metrics.metric: Answers that contradict each other or are out of date, found in a one-time audit
success_metrics.baseline: Not counted today. The audit produces the baseline. One item is visible from outside already (c14 versus c19).
success_metrics.target: 100 percent of items found are corrected or carry a named owner and a due date by end of week 6, and the aurora dates are published as ONE range before August 21.
success_metrics.timeframe: Aurora dates before August 21. Everything else by end of week 6.

success_metrics.metric: Guest complaints traced to a policy answer, THE GUARDRAIL, because speeding up a wrong answer is worse than doing nothing
success_metrics.baseline: None exists in comparable form. Counted for two weeks before anything changes.
success_metrics.target: No increase, and any complaint traced to a card corrected within one business day with the correction visible in the change log.

key_dependencies: The returning-versus-new split on the summer roster, from payroll rehire flags, BEFORE pricing.
A named owner with authority to settle a disputed answer, at kickoff.
Two to four hours with a veteran and a supervisor at each of the three properties, weeks 2-3.
Whatever internal procedure and training material exists, week 1. This is the single biggest reason the fee moves from 18,000 toward 26,000.
A decision on the correct aurora date range, before August 21.
Permission to run paper tally sheets at three desks for two weeks, week 1, BEFORE any building starts.

top_risks.risk: The summer roster is mostly returning staff, not first-time hires. The time-to-competence case collapses.
top_risks.mitigation: Asked before pricing, not during a paid phase. One email retires it. If mostly returning, we cut the fee and the scope and DROP the onboarding metric rather than restating it as something softer.

top_risks.risk: The thing that gets used is the printed sheet, not the software. We would have sold a system and delivered a piece of paper.
top_risks.mitigation: We think this is the likely outcome and have designed for it. The shift sheet is a first-class deliverable. If the search side goes unused the log will show it and the readout will say so, which is also the strongest argument against funding anything smarter.

top_risks.risk: Habit beats us. Asking the veteran standing next to you is faster than any lookup.
top_risks.mitigation: Nothing beats turning your head, and a proposal claiming otherwise would be lying. What this beats is the three cases where turning your head fails.

top_risks.risk: A large share of what the desk gets asked is live status, which this never answers.
top_risks.mitigation: Stated up front as a permanent limit. The tally sheets will show what share it is, and that number is theirs to keep.

roi.case_shape: A break-even threshold case, not a projection. Every input a savings model needs is missing and we refuse to invent any of it. The table answers a different question, one they can falsify in a week on their own desk: how much would this have to prevent, per shift, before it has paid for itself.
roi.headline_honesty: THE CONSERVATIVE CASE DOES NOT CLEAR ON PREVENTED INTERRUPTIONS ALONE, and that is stated in the section heading rather than a footnote. It recovers 43 percent of five-year cost on labour. What it clears is the bar the economics pre-check actually set, a durable artifact plus four gating baselines at a small fixed fee. Rigging the drivers upward to make labour clear would be the exact reverse-engineering the section exists to refuse.
roi.value_owner: The Operations Manager owns the number, with one front-desk supervisor at the pilot property owning the cards day to day. We name the ROLE and not a person, because the only source for who holds it is a 2018 profile and eight years is long enough that we will not assume.
roi.variance_check: One week of paper tally BEFORE anything is built, which costs nothing and is the baseline. The same tally at 30, 90 and 180 days, with hard checkpoints at the August 21 flip and the mid-September close. At 90 days, compare actual prevented interruptions per shift against the conservative driver of 2. If actual is below it, the labour argument is wrong, we say so in writing, and Desk Search does not get funded.
roi.what_would_make_this_not_worth_it: Four honest ways this is a bad buy. If the paper tally shows the desk almost never escalates, the capacity line is near zero and only the artifact and baselines remain. If the questions are mostly live-status questions, a card set can't answer them and never will. If the summer roster is mostly returning staff, the prize shrinks and the ask should shrink with it. If nobody will own the roughly 48 hours a year of upkeep, do not start. There is also a version that costs nothing: run the paper tally yourselves for a week and fix the aurora date on your own two pages. If that is enough, keep your money.

now: The one question we ask before you are quoted, the returning share of the summer front-of-house roster.
One audit of every answer you publish, across three properties and both seasons.
Turn what you already publish into cards with a property tag, a date range, a source and a last-reviewed date.
Capture the operating long tail that is not on your website. This slice is what moves the fee inside the band.
The printed shift sheet, summer version and aurora version, taped to each desk.
Run the set through the August 21 flip with supervisors tagging what still gets escalated.
Handoff. Name the owner, hand over the card set, the change log, the sheets and a plain export.
next: Desk Search, funded ONLY if the log shows a repeating population of real questions no card and no combination of cards serves. If the log says the cards and the paper were enough, we tell you the search box is not needed and quote you nothing.
Scenario cards for multi-part questions that actually recur. If they recur, the cheaper and more testable answer is more editorial work in your own voice, not software.
later: Housekeeping route optimisation, BOUGHT from an established vendor, piloted on one property before three, modelled only on their own occupancy and loaded labour rate.
The corporate and extended-stay path, gated on one measurement only they can make.
Structured arrival intake for the courtesy van, a form and a dispatch board, EXPLICITLY not a voice agent.
Sorting and routing on the general inbox.
The named owner and the review cadence, run forever at boundaries they already publish.
roadmap.gates_summary: Five gates, each one their off-ramp. Before pricing (zero cost, they keep the number). After the audit (they keep the full list and one canonical aurora date range, and can fix their own pages and never speak to us again). After the cards and sheets exist (they keep the whole card set permanently, no licence, nothing that switches off). After the flip run, which is the funding gate for Desk Search (they keep four baselines and the question log, including the parts that argue against buying anything else from us). Handoff.
roadmap.handoff_ongoing_cost: A named person's time, not software. Realistically a couple of hours at each season boundary plus a few minutes whenever a policy changes. The failure mode is not cost, it is that the owner's name quietly goes unfilled and the set decays the way binders decay. If nobody will genuinely own it, say so at the first gate and do not start.
